## 🎯 The task

This is the first of five **challenges**. From today you have your own time series, and one number
to beat on it.

Forecast the next $h$ observations of your series and beat your benchmark — with the toolbox from
Week 3 and nothing more. No ETS, no ARIMA: those are the next challenges, and this one is the
measurement that makes their improvement visible.

::: {.callout-important}
## This one counts

8 points. **Deadline: 23:59 today**, on Moodle. The accuracy score is published the next morning;
rubric marks and comments come back before the next practice session.
:::

## 🗂 Your series

Your series is issued by a hash of the **same identifier you have used since Week 1**. The template
does it for you: it turns your identifier into a code such as `TS-4DD7A` and downloads that series.

::: {.callout-note}
## What "anonymised" means here

The series is real. What has been removed is its identity: no name, no units, values rescaled,
the calendar shifted by whole years, the history trimmed. Two students never get the same window of
the same series, so a forecast is worth exactly what your model is worth.

You are not expected to work out what it measures, and you will not be marked for trying. Read the
data, not the domain.
:::

**This series is yours for the rest of the course.** Challenges 2–5 (ETS, ARIMA, seasonal ARIMA,
advanced methods) run on the same series, so you will watch your own forecast improve — or fail to.

## 📊 Section 1 — EDA and visualisation (1 point)

One point, and it is not a repeat of Lab 2: this is a **new series**, and the plots are here to
support the choice of method.

- A time plot, and whichever of the seasonal / subseries / ACF plots your argument actually uses.
- Every plot needs a sentence. A plot with no reading attached earns nothing.
- Show the validation split on a plot: history, validation window, and your forecast over it.

## 📐 Section 2 — Forecast and accuracy (3 points)

### Your benchmark

The benchmark is the **best of the four simple methods** from Week 1 — `mean`, `naive`, `snaive`,
`drift` — chosen on a validation window: the last $h$ observations of the history you were given.

Nothing about it is hidden. The template computes it, and the scorer computes it the same way, from
the same public data:

1. fit the four methods to everything except the last $h$ observations;
2. score them on those $h$ observations by RMSE, and keep the winner;
3. refit the winner on the **whole** history you were given — that is your benchmark.

### How the points are awarded

Your forecast and the benchmark's are both scored by **MASE** on the $h$ observations that come
after your history, which you have not seen.

$$
\text{skill} = \frac{\text{MASE}_{\text{you}}}{\text{MASE}_{\text{benchmark}}}
$$

| Result | Points |
|---|---:|
| skill $\le 1.00$ — you beat the benchmark | 3 |
| skill $\le 1.10$ — within 10% of it | 2 |
| worse than that | 1, and Section 3 must say why |

::: {.callout-note}
## Your series is known to be beatable

Every series in the pool was screened: it is only issued if a reference model lands between
**0.70 and 0.90** of its benchmark. Below that the series is trivial, above it effectively
unbeatable. If you do not beat your benchmark, that is a fact about your model, not your luck.

The screening reference was an automatic ETS or ARIMA — models you meet in the next two challenges.
With the toolbox alone, matching the benchmark is a solid result and beating it is a good one.
:::

### What the toolbox gives you {.smaller}

Everything in this list is Week 3 material, and each of them can beat a simple method:

- a **transformation** — Box-Cox, if the seasonal swing grows with the level;
- **forecasting with decomposition**: STL the series, forecast the seasonally adjusted part with
  `naive` or `drift`, carry the seasonal component forward with `snaive`, add them back;
- a **combination**: the average of two or three forecasts is often better than any of them;
- **residual diagnostics** to catch a model that is leaving structure behind.

📖 [FPP 5.7 forecasting with decomposition](https://otexts.com/fpp3/forecasting-decomposition.html) ·
[FPP 5.4 residual diagnostics](https://otexts.com/fpp3/diagnostics.html) ·
[FPP 5.8 evaluating accuracy](https://otexts.com/fpp3/accuracy.html) ·
[FPP the Pythonic Way, ch. 5](https://otexts.com/fpppy/nbs/05-toolbox.html)

## ✍️ Section 3 — Justification block (3 points)

Three points, and the only part of the work a human reads closely. Four things, roughly a paragraph
each:

| Item | Points | What earns them |
|---|---:|---|
| 3.1 What the data shows | 0.75 | Frequency, seasonal period, trend, level shifts, outliers — with the plot that shows each claim |
| 3.2 Why this method | 0.75 | The method you submitted and **why it fits what you just described**, including what you tried and dropped |
| 3.3 What the residuals say | 0.75 | ACF and a Ljung-Box test on your final model's residuals, read — what structure is left, and whether it matters at this horizon |
| 3.4 What you expect | 0.75 | Your own MASE on the validation window against the benchmark's, and the number you expect on the hidden holdout |

::: {.callout-important}
Marked on the reasoning, not on the outcome. A well-argued forecast that loses to the benchmark
scores full marks in Section 3 — and if it loses, say what you think the holdout contained that your
validation window did not.
:::

## 🧹 Section 4 — Code quality and reproducibility (1 point)

- The notebook runs top to bottom on a fresh kernel without errors.
- Your submission file is written **by the notebook**, not edited by hand.
- No leakage: nothing after the end of your history exists, so nothing can be fitted to it. If you
  tune on the validation window, say so in 3.2 — that is legitimate, and it is also why your
  validation MASE is optimistic.

## 📤 Submission

Upload three files to the Week 4 activity on Moodle **before 23:59 today**:

- `SURNAME_ch1_forecast.csv` — written by the last cell of the template. Exactly $h$ rows and these
  columns:

  | Column | What |
  |---|---|
  | `student_id` | your identifier |
  | `code` | your series code, e.g. `TS-4DD7A` |
  | `ds` | the dates you are forecasting, in order |
  | `yhat` | your point forecast |
  | `yhat_lo_80`, `yhat_hi_80` | your 80% interval — not marked this week, but the scorer records its coverage |

- `SURNAME_ch1.pdf` — the report, with the justification block;
- `SURNAME_ch1.ipynb` — the source.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The scorer is strict about the format, and only about the format

Wrong dates, wrong number of rows, a missing column or a `NaN` in `yhat` cannot be scored, and
Section 1 is then 0. The template writes the file correctly; if you rebuild it by hand, run the
check cell it provides.
:::
